# Owner interaction preferences

Personal preferences from the repo owner for how the assistant should interact — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, how results and decisions are surfaced, and the phrases the owner uses to trigger defined commands. These are **not** project conventions (those live in the [packs/](../packs/) corpus, each pack bundling its skills); they're how the owner likes to be worked with. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the entry here just owns the trigger phrase.

## Preferences

- **When there's nothing left to do, say so boldly at the end of the conversation.** Don't bury a "this is complete / I'm blocked / nothing further to do" behind hedging — make the terminal state unmistakable. **Set it apart visually so it catches the eye:** put the terminal state — or, when work remains, the list of open/outstanding items — in its own callout (a Markdown blockquote box, e.g. `> ✅ All done` or `> ⚠️ Still open: …`), not trailing prose the owner has to scan for. One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does.
- **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md](../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`.
- **"bump version"** is the owner's phrase for raising a project's version (a minor bump by default). It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc.
- **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control.
- **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.)
- **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of.
- **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. This composes with the enclose-the-whole-thing preference above: the disclaimer sits inside the same delimited block as the prompt it prefixes.
- **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked.
# Claudinite — active-pack guidance

The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand.

<!-- pack:basics -->
# Working discipline

The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.

Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better.

Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix.

1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.

The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.

Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided.

When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.

When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."

Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.

Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere.

Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.

When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.

An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.

# The task lifecycle

The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.

For every new task:

1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.

---

<!-- pack:tidy-repo -->
# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy

The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the
pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is
the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills
([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)).

The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**

- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
  ref's auto-generated name.
- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.

Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites
**its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body
rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the
three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body.

---

<!-- pack:laughcounter -->
# Working in this repo

The general lessons this repo has paid for once. The privacy boundary — the
product's defining constraint — has its own pack (`local/on-device-privacy`);
what follows is everything else.

**Don't prune a `.gitignore` section in the same breath as deleting what it
ignored — the artifacts are still on disk.** Removing a toolchain (the Python
reference, a build system, a generator) invites tidying its ignore rules away in
the same commit, but the ignored artifacts it already produced are usually still
sitting untracked in the worktree — earlier test runs leave `__pycache__/`,
builds leave `build/`. The moment those rules go, the next `git add -A` sweeps
the artifacts *into* the very commit that was supposed to remove them, and
nothing complains: the commit is valid, the tests still pass, and the junk only
shows up as an inflated file count in the diff a reviewer reads. Delete the
artifacts from the worktree first (or `git clean` them), then drop their ignore
lines — and read `git diff --cached --stat` after any bulk `git add -A`, not just
`git status`, since staged additions are exactly what a clean `git status` stops
telling you about.

---

<!-- pack:on-device-privacy -->
# On-device privacy — the boundary the whole product is built around

An always-on microphone in someone's living room only earns its place if what it
hears stays on the machine. That promise is the product requirement
(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, README *Privacy*), the text of the mic and
speech prompts users actually see (`mac/Resources/Info.plist`), and the reason
several design choices look heavier than they need to. The checks in this pack
hold the mechanical half; what follows is the judgment half.

There is now exactly one implementation — the native app in `mac/Sources/` — so
every rule below is about it.

**What may cross the boundary: derived metadata, never audio.** A laugh is
persisted as time, duration, confidence, and an origin label — that is what the
JSONL lines carry, and `LaughStore` says so in its own header. **No audio is
stored at all** — the `no-audio-persistence` check holds this mechanically for
v1. A feature that wants to keep audio (the v3 roadmap's rolling buffer) is not
a new field, it is a new promise to the user: it changes the mic prompt and this
check together, in the same PR.

**Everything lives in one deletable directory.**
`~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/` holds the laugh log and the app's
own diagnostic log, and nothing lands outside it (the one path macOS dictates, not
us, is a Login Item registration). "Delete the folder and it's gone" is a promise a
user *acts on* — someone who deletes it believes the mic's whole memory of them
went with it. So a feature needing somewhere new to keep things extends that
directory rather than earning a second one.

**There is no accepted egress — none.** Detection (Sound Analysis) and speech
recognition (`SFSpeechRecognizer` with on-device recognition required) are both
built into macOS; no model is downloaded, no telemetry is sent, and the app makes
no outbound connection of any kind. The `no-network-client` check is therefore
absolute rather than carve-out-shaped. Adding *any* egress — a model fetch, a
crash reporter, a sync feature — is a product decision that gets written here and
in the README *Privacy* section before a line of it is written in Swift.

**There is no server either.** The app listens on no socket. The web dashboard
that once existed in the Python reference was removed on purpose, along with the
reference itself. Reintroducing any listener — a dashboard, a metrics port, a
remote-control API — is a decision about exposing the laugh log, not a feature to
slip in: it needs the owner's explicit sign-off, a loopback-only default, and a
story for authentication or CSRF before it lands.

**The disclosure must stay true.** `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and
`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` tell the user audio is analysed on-device
and not recorded. If the app's behaviour ever changes, those strings change with
it in the same commit — a stale privacy prompt is worse than a blunt one.

## github
The GitHub MCP Server provides tools to interact with GitHub platform.

Tool selection guidance:
	1. Use 'list_*' tools for broad, simple retrieval and pagination of all items of a type (e.g., all issues, all PRs, all branches) with basic filtering.
	2. Use 'search_*' tools for targeted queries with specific criteria, keywords, or complex filters (e.g., issues with certain text, PRs by author, code containing functions).

Context management:
	1. Use pagination whenever possible with batches of 5-10 items.
	2. Use minimal_output parameter set to true if the full information is not needed to accomplish a task.

Tool usage guidance:
	1. For 'search_*' tools: Use separate 'sort' and 'order' parameters if available for sorting results - do not include 'sort:' syntax in query strings. Query strings should contain only search criteria (e.g., 'org:google language:python'), not sorting instructions. Always call 'get_me' first to understand current user permissions and context. ## Issues

Check 'list_issue_types' first for organizations to use proper issue types. Use 'search_issues' before creating new issues to avoid duplicates. Always set 'state_reason' when closing issues. ## Pull Requests

PR review workflow: Always use 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'create' to create a pending review, then 'add_comment_to_pending_review' to add comments, and finally 'pull_request_review_write' with method 'submit_pending' to submit the review for complex reviews with line-specific comments.

Before creating a pull request, search for pull request templates in the repository. Template files are called pull_request_template.md or they're located in '.github/PULL_REQUEST_TEMPLATE' directory. Use the template content to structure the PR description and then call create_pull_request tool.

# Prose-to-checks — sweep this repo's pack prose

Mine the **existing** prose of this repo's packs — each pack's `RULES.md` / `SKILL.md` — for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Where [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md) descends the ladder for each *new* lesson, this task works the *backlog*: standing prose that was always mechanizable but never converted.

You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue whose **Context section is binding scope**: it names the **pack paths** to sweep. Work only those paths — a consuming repo's own local packs by default; Claudinite also its core `packs/`. **Never** edit a read-only mounted canon pack under `.claudinite/shared/`.

The task's declared outcome ceiling is **`open-pr`**: convert prose to checks in a single owner-approved PR (a check can break CI or misfire, so it is reviewed, not auto-merged).

## The method lives in the skill

The conversion method — how to spot an always-testable rule in prose, judge convertibility, author the check plus its **see-it-fail** fixture, and decide what stays prose — is owned by the [**prose-to-checks** skill](../../skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md). Follow it; don't re-derive it here. This worker only frames the unattended run around it.

## What a run does

1. **Pick convertible prose** under the Context's pack paths — rules that are *always testable* (a deterministic condition a check could assert) and that no existing check already covers. Prefer the strongest, clearest candidates; converting one or two solid rules well beats churning many shakily.
2. **Convert per the skill** — author the rule module in its owning pack, register it in that pack's `pack.mjs`, and add a **fixture test that fires on a violating input and stays quiet on a clean one** (see-it-fail is mandatory — a check that can't be made confident is left as prose, never shipped broken). Trim the now-redundant prose to rationale.
3. **Open a PR** — one PR for the run's conversions on a per-run-unique branch, its commit referencing the tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes. Keep the repo's offline test suite green before opening.
4. **Log to the tracker** — the standing log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Prose to Checks`** in this repo. Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number**; create it already closed if missing. **Never open, close, or reopen it**. Log each run as a **dated comment**: the prose converted and the check id it became, or "nothing convertible this run".

## What this task must never do

- **Never ship a check that can't be made confident** — the see-it-fail fixture is the gate; an unprovable rule stays prose.
- **Never convert a rule an existing check already covers** — dedupe against the check set first.
- **Never touch a pack path outside the Context**, and **never edit a mounted canon pack** under `.claudinite/shared/` — a consumer improves only its own local packs.
- **Run on `opus`** — judging convertibility and authoring checks + fixtures is heavy judgment; this task declares `agent_model: opus`.

19	prose under those paths (each pack's `RULES.md`, and any `SKILL.md` beside them). Never edit a
20	read-only mounted canon pack under `.claudinite/shared/`.
21

23	
24	For each rule, ask the one question from
25	[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
26	signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**
27	
28	- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
29	  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
30	- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),

32	  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.

5	(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, README *Privacy*), the text of the mic and
6	speech prompts users actually see (`mac/Resources/Info.plist`), and the reason

9

11	every rule below is about it.
12

18	a new field, it is a new promise to the user: it changes the mic prompt and this
19	check together, in the same PR.
20

23	own diagnostic log, and nothing lands outside it (the one path macOS dictates, not
24	us, is a Login Item registration). "Delete the folder and it's gone" is a promise a

26	went with it. So a feature needing somewhere new to keep things extends that

# On-device privacy — the boundary the whole product is built around

An always-on microphone in someone's living room only earns its place if what it
hears stays on the machine. That promise is the product requirement
(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, README *Privacy*), the text of the mic and
speech prompts users actually see (`mac/Resources/Info.plist`), and the reason
several design choices look heavier than they need to. The checks in this pack
hold the mechanical half; what follows is the judgment half.

There is now exactly one implementation — the native app in `mac/Sources/` — so
every rule below is about it.

**What may cross the boundary: derived metadata, never audio.** A laugh is
persisted as time, duration, confidence, and an origin label — that is what the
JSONL lines carry, and `LaughStore` says so in its own header. **No audio is
stored at all** — the `no-audio-persistence` check holds this mechanically for
v1. A feature that wants to keep audio (the v3 roadmap's rolling buffer) is not
a new field, it is a new promise to the user: it changes the mic prompt and this
check together, in the same PR.

**Everything lives in one deletable directory.**
`~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/` holds the laugh log and the app's
own diagnostic log, and nothing lands outside it (the one path macOS dictates, not
us, is a Login Item registration). "Delete the folder and it's gone" is a promise a
user *acts on* — someone who deletes it believes the mic's whole memory of them
went with it. So a feature needing somewhere new to keep things extends that
directory rather than earning a second one.

**There is no accepted egress — none.** Detection (Sound Analysis) and speech
recognition (`SFSpeechRecognizer` with on-device recognition required) are both
built into macOS; no model is downloaded, no telemetry is sent, and the app makes
no outbound connection of any kind. The `no-network-client` check is therefore
absolute rather than carve-out-shaped. Adding *any* egress — a model fetch, a
crash reporter, a sync feature — is a product decision that gets written here and
in the README *Privacy* section before a line of it is written in Swift.

**There is no server either.** The app listens on no socket. The web dashboard
that once existed in the Python reference was removed on purpose, along with the
reference itself. Reintroducing any listener — a dashboard, a metrics port, a
remote-control API — is a decision about exposing the laugh log, not a feature to
slip in: it needs the owner's explicit sign-off, a loopback-only default, and a
story for authentication or CSRF before it lands.

**The disclosure must stay true.** `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and
`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` tell the user audio is analysed on-device
and not recorded. If the app's behaviour ever changes, those strings change with
it in the same commit — a stale privacy prompt is worse than a blunt one.

7	// product requirements (docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md §0/§6) and the README's
8	// Privacy section state it; nothing enforced it until this pack. It covers the
9	// native app (mac/Sources/), which is the whole product.
10	//
11	// A local pack: declared by hand as `local/on-device-privacy`, never
12	// fingerprinted (detect/marker null).
13	export default {
14	  id: 'on-device-privacy',
15	  detect: null,
16	  marker: null,

Converted **two** prose rules; PR #51 (open for review).

| Prose converted (`on-device-privacy/RULES.md`) | Check id |
| --- | --- |
| "the mutating endpoints require an `application/json` content type… Any new mutating endpoint keeps that guard" | `on-device-privacy/json-content-type-guard` (blocking) |
| "Everything lives in one deletable directory… don't scatter state (caches, model files, logs) outside it" | `on-device-privacy/single-home-dir` (blocking) |

Two notes worth carrying forward:

- **`json-content-type-guard` only became confident once it parsed instead of grepped.** `dashboard.py` contains `application/json` nine times — eight response content types plus the inline page's `fetch()` — so a text grep passes a handler that has no guard at all. Slicing the `do_POST`/`PUT`/`PATCH`/`DELETE` body by indentation and requiring the guard *inside it* kills that. A fixture pins the false alarm directly.
- **`single-home-dir` needed a mandated-location exemption to ship.** Its first run fired on `cli.py`'s `~/Library/LaunchAgents/{label}.plist` — a true positive by pattern, a false alarm by rule: launchd dictates that path, and `cmd_service` already sends the agent's log back to `home_path`, so the "delete the folder and it's gone" promise still holds. Exemption list kept deliberately short — a cache or model dir is a choice, and a choice belongs under the home directory.

Left as prose (judgment about meaning, not a static signature): "metadata persists, audio doesn't"; "the model download is the only egress"; "the `NS*UsageDescription` strings stay true". Also left: absolute paths outside `$HOME` and the app's `~/Library/Application Support/` directory, which `single-home-dir` explicitly does not claim.

Fixtures: `node --test .claudinite/local/packs/on-device-privacy/pack.test.mjs` → 12/12 (6 new); `check_the_world` clean with both rules registered.

Swept `.claudinite/local/packs` (the only local pack is `on-device-privacy`). Two `RULES.md` rules were always-testable and uncovered by the existing three checks; both converted in #54.

| Prose converted | Check id |
| --- | --- |
| "Everything lives in one deletable directory" (`~/.laughcounter`, `~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/`) | `on-device-privacy/single-home-directory` |
| "Any new mutating endpoint keeps that [`application/json`] guard" | `on-device-privacy/json-content-type-guard` |

Both blocking, both with a fixture that fires on a violation and stays quiet on the real tree, and both additionally seen to fail against the **real** sources under a realistic regression (home moved to `~/.cache`; `Store.swift`'s `LaughCounter` narrowing dropped; `.cachesDirectory` substituted; `dashboard.py`'s guard deleted, its body read hoisted above the guard, and an unguarded `do_DELETE` added). `single-home-directory` carries one documented exemption, `~/Library/LaunchAgents` — launchd mandates that location and the app only prints the plist.

Prose trimmed to rationale in `RULES.md`; `README.md`'s enforcement table updated.

Left as prose, with reasons: *metadata persists, audio doesn't* (judgment about a new field's meaning), *the model download is the only accepted egress* (the negative half is already `no-network-client`; the positive half is a decision), and *the disclosure must stay true* (the enforceable "the usage strings exist" is a weaker, different rule than "they change in the same commit as the behaviour" — which leaves no artifact to scan).

PR opened, not merged — outcome ceiling `open-pr`.

Swept `.claudinite/local/packs` (the only local pack is `on-device-privacy`). Converted **one** prose rule; PR #69 (open for review).

| Prose converted (`on-device-privacy/RULES.md`) | Check id |
| --- | --- |
| "No audio is stored at all" | `on-device-privacy/no-audio-persistence` (blocking) |

Two prior runs (#51, #54) both considered this rule and left it as prose, reasoning that "does this new persisted field carry audio" is a judgment about meaning, not a static signature. That's correct as far as it goes — but it isn't the only way to hold the rule. This conversion sidesteps field-classification entirely and bans the **known audio-file-writing APIs** directly (`AVAudioFile(forWriting:)`, `AVAudioRecorder`, `ExtAudioFileCreateWithURL`, `AudioFileCreateWithURL`) in `mac/Sources/**.swift` — the same absolute-ban-list shape `no-network-client` already uses for egress. `AVAudioFile(forReading:)` is deliberately excluded (a bundled sound asset load isn't persistence); a fixture pins that non-finding.

Noted in the check and RULES.md: this holds for **v1** only — the roadmap's v3 deliberately adds a rolling audio buffer, and landing that updates this check (and the mic usage strings) in the same PR, exactly as `no-network-client` already expects of a deliberate future egress decision.

Left as prose, with reasons (unchanged from prior runs, re-verified this run): *one deletable directory* (would need data-flow tracking of a `FileManager` write target back to its declaration to be confident — not just a token grep); *no egress at all* / *no server or listener* (already covered by `no-network-client`, which bans `import Network` outright); *the disclosure must stay true* (judgment about prompt accuracy, and "same commit as the behaviour" is diff-shaped, not scannable from file content alone).

Fixtures: `node --test .claudinite/local/packs/on-device-privacy/pack.test.mjs` → 7/7 (3 new). `run-active-pack-rules.mjs`, `check_the_world.mjs`, `check_the_work.mjs` all exit 0 with the new rule registered.

PR opened, not merged — outcome ceiling `open-pr`.

1	# Prose-to-checks — sweep this repo's pack prose
2	
3	Mine the **existing** prose of this repo's packs — each pack's `RULES.md` / `SKILL.md` — for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Where [growth-extract](../growth-extract/task.md) descends the ladder for each *new* lesson, this task works the *backlog*: standing prose that was always mechanizable but never converted.
4	
5	You run under the executor, dispatched by a `ready-for-agent` issue whose **Context section is binding scope**: it names the **pack paths** to sweep. Work only those paths — a consuming repo's own local packs by default; Claudinite also its core `packs/`. **Never** edit a read-only mounted canon pack under `.claudinite/shared/`.
6	
7	The task's declared outcome ceiling is **`open-pr`**: convert prose to checks in a single owner-approved PR (a check can break CI or misfire, so it is reviewed, not auto-merged).
8	
9	## The method lives in the skill
10	
11	The conversion method — how to spot an always-testable rule in prose, judge convertibility, author the check plus its **see-it-fail** fixture, and decide what stays prose — is owned by the [**prose-to-checks** skill](../../skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md). Follow it; don't re-derive it here. This worker only frames the unattended run around it.
12	
13	## What a run does
14	
15	1. **Pick convertible prose** under the Context's pack paths — rules that are *always testable* (a deterministic condition a check could assert) and that no existing check already covers. Prefer the strongest, clearest candidates; converting one or two solid rules well beats churning many shakily.
16	2. **Convert per the skill** — author the rule module in its owning pack, register it in that pack's `pack.mjs`, and add a **fixture test that fires on a violating input and stays quiet on a clean one** (see-it-fail is mandatory — a check that can't be made confident is left as prose, never shipped broken). Trim the now-redundant prose to rationale.
17	3. **Open a PR** — one PR for the run's conversions on a per-run-unique branch, its commit referencing the tracking issue so the `task-lifecycle` gate passes. Keep the repo's offline test suite green before opening.
18	4. **Log to the tracker** — the standing log is the issue titled exactly **`Claudinite tracker: Prose to Checks`** in this repo. Find it **by that exact title, never a fuzzy match or a hard-coded number**; create it already closed if missing. **Never open, close, or reopen it**. Log each run as a **dated comment**: the prose converted and the check id it became, or "nothing convertible this run".
19	
20	## What this task must never do
21	
22	- **Never ship a check that can't be made confident** — the see-it-fail fixture is the gate; an unprovable rule stays prose.
23	- **Never convert a rule an existing check already covers** — dedupe against the check set first.
24	- **Never touch a pack path outside the Context**, and **never edit a mounted canon pack** under `.claudinite/shared/` — a consumer improves only its own local packs.
25	- **Run on `opus`** — judging convertibility and authoring checks + fixtures is heavy judgment; this task declares `agent_model: opus`.
26

2	name: prose-to-checks
3	description: Mine a repo's existing pack prose (RULES.md, SKILL.md) for always-testable rules that were never converted to checks, and convert the strongest ones. Use when auditing packs for convertible rules, or when the growth prose-to-checks sweep runs.
4	---
5	
6	# Convert existing prose to checks
7	
8	A completeness-critic over a repo's own packs. The growth *extract* stage converts each **new**
9	lesson down the promotion ladder; this pass sweeps the **existing** prose backlog for rules that
10	are always-testable but still live only as prose — and converts them, so the packs keep shedding
11	context over time instead of only at the moment a rule is first learned. It runs as
12	grow_with_claudinite's daily `prose-to-checks-sweep` task, and on demand.
13	
14	## Scope — the pack paths you were given
15	
16	Work only the **pack paths configured for this repo** (the task passes them in its Context): a
17	consuming repo's own **local packs** (`.claudinite/local/packs/`) by default — projects don't
18	improve core canon packs — while **Claudinite itself** also sweeps its core `packs/`. Read the
19	prose under those paths (each pack's `RULES.md`, and any `SKILL.md` beside them). Never edit a
20	read-only mounted canon pack under `.claudinite/shared/`.
21	
22	## What to look for — the check-the-world test
23	
24	For each rule, ask the one question from
25	[engine/checks/DESIGN.md](../../../../engine/checks/DESIGN.md): **does it constrain a *static
26	signature in the repo artifact* — something a post-hoc scan could observe?**
27	
28	- **Yes → a conversion candidate.** A dangling-reference rule, a filename convention, a workflow
29	  or manifest shape, a "these two files must agree" invariant, a forbidden pattern in code.
30	- **No → leave it.** In-flight process (leaves no artifact — "see the test fail first"),
31	  judgment ("name by scope"), or knowledge whose failure is only visible at runtime (jsdom
32	  diverging from Chrome). These are why the rule is prose; don't force them.
33	
34	The check-the-world rule from DESIGN holds: if a rule is always-testable, it was never really
35	part of the on-demand skill — it belongs in a pack as a check.
36	
37	## How to convert one
38	
39	Follow the extract stage's check-authoring discipline (the local promotion ladder in
40	[extracting-lessons.md](../../extracting-lessons.md)). For each candidate:
41	
42	1. **Author the check** in the owning pack (`<pack>/<rule>.mjs`, listed in its `pack.mjs`) — the
43	   failure message *is* the rule (what / why / fix / `doc:` pointer back to the prose).
44	2. **Write the fixture first and see it fail** — a violating fixture must find, a clean one must
45	   not (the test lives beside the pack's other tests). A conversion with no proving fixture
46	   doesn't ship.
47	3. **Ship at real severity, fail-fast** — blocking for a defect, advisory only when the rule is
48	   directional by kind.
49	4. **Trim the prose** to rationale — the check owns enforcement now; leaving both pays twice and
50	   springs the drift trap.
51	
52	**Before writing a rule off as un-checkable, try parsing the file's structure instead of grepping
53	its text.** Grep finds the pattern anywhere; parsing finds it in the one spot the rule means —
54	which kills the false alarm. (Example: `Authorization` is only wrong inside a CloudFront policy's
55	*own* header list, not elsewhere in the template.) Parse only as much as you need, and hold the
56	check to the same fixture bar.
57	
58	When even a scoped parser can't make detection confident, **leave the prose and log the
59	candidate** to a tagged conversion-backlog issue rather than shipping a shaky check.
60	
61	## Bounds
62	
63	- **One PR, bounded surface** — the new rule module, its `pack.mjs` line, its fixture, and the
64	  trimmed prose. Don't "improve" unrelated rules while you're in there.
65	- **Never delete a rule you didn't convert** — trimming prose is only for a rule a *landed* check
66	  now enforces.
67	- Run the suite and the sweep green before opening the PR; open it for the owner's approval,
68	  never a direct push to `main`.

1	# On-device privacy — the boundary the whole product is built around
2	
3	An always-on microphone in someone's living room only earns its place if what it
4	hears stays on the machine. That promise is the product requirement
5	(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, README *Privacy*), the text of the mic and
6	speech prompts users actually see (`mac/Resources/Info.plist`), and the reason
7	several design choices look heavier than they need to. The checks in this pack
8	hold the mechanical half; what follows is the judgment half.
9	
10	There is now exactly one implementation — the native app in `mac/Sources/` — so
11	every rule below is about it.
12	
13	**What may cross the boundary: derived metadata, never audio.** A laugh is
14	persisted as time, duration, confidence, and an origin label — that is what the
15	JSONL lines carry, and `LaughStore` says so in its own header. **No audio is
16	stored at all** — the `no-audio-persistence` check holds this mechanically for
17	v1. A feature that wants to keep audio (the v3 roadmap's rolling buffer) is not
18	a new field, it is a new promise to the user: it changes the mic prompt and this
19	check together, in the same PR.
20	
21	**Everything lives in one deletable directory.**
22	`~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/` holds the laugh log and the app's
23	own diagnostic log, and nothing lands outside it (the one path macOS dictates, not
24	us, is a Login Item registration). "Delete the folder and it's gone" is a promise a
25	user *acts on* — someone who deletes it believes the mic's whole memory of them
26	went with it. So a feature needing somewhere new to keep things extends that
27	directory rather than earning a second one.
28	
29	**There is no accepted egress — none.** Detection (Sound Analysis) and speech
30	recognition (`SFSpeechRecognizer` with on-device recognition required) are both
31	built into macOS; no model is downloaded, no telemetry is sent, and the app makes
32	no outbound connection of any kind. The `no-network-client` check is therefore
33	absolute rather than carve-out-shaped. Adding *any* egress — a model fetch, a
34	crash reporter, a sync feature — is a product decision that gets written here and
35	in the README *Privacy* section before a line of it is written in Swift.
36	
37	**There is no server either.** The app listens on no socket. The web dashboard
38	that once existed in the Python reference was removed on purpose, along with the
39	reference itself. Reintroducing any listener — a dashboard, a metrics port, a
40	remote-control API — is a decision about exposing the laugh log, not a feature to
41	slip in: it needs the owner's explicit sign-off, a loopback-only default, and a
42	story for authentication or CSRF before it lands.
43	
44	**The disclosure must stay true.** `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and
45	`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` tell the user audio is analysed on-device
46	and not recorded. If the app's behaviour ever changes, those strings change with
47	it in the same commit — a stale privacy prompt is worse than a blunt one.
48

1	# Working in this repo
2	
3	The general lessons this repo has paid for once. The privacy boundary — the
4	product's defining constraint — has its own pack (`local/on-device-privacy`);
5	what follows is everything else.
6	
7	**Don't prune a `.gitignore` section in the same breath as deleting what it
8	ignored — the artifacts are still on disk.** Removing a toolchain (the Python
9	reference, a build system, a generator) invites tidying its ignore rules away in
10	the same commit, but the ignored artifacts it already produced are usually still
11	sitting untracked in the worktree — earlier test runs leave `__pycache__/`,
12	builds leave `build/`. The moment those rules go, the next `git add -A` sweeps
13	the artifacts *into* the very commit that was supposed to remove them, and
14	nothing complains: the commit is valid, the tests still pass, and the junk only
15	shows up as an inflated file count in the diff a reviewer reads. Delete the
16	artifacts from the worktree first (or `git clean` them), then drop their ignore
17	lines — and read `git diff --cached --stat` after any bulk `git add -A`, not just
18	`git status`, since staged additions are exactly what a clean `git status` stops
19	telling you about.

One or the other always gets the box: the done-signal when nothing remains, the open-items list when something does.
- **"LGTM"** is the owner's phrase for the merge-to-main command: it asks for the change in front of the owner to be merged into `main`. It's an owner-triggered command; the default mechanics live in the `merge-to-main` skill ([../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md](../packs/git-github/skills/merge-to-main/SKILL.md)) (squash, gate on CI only when the repo has it), and a project that diverges overrides them via a bespoke merge-policy file it names in its own `CLAUDE.md`.
- **"bump version"** is the owner's phrase for raising a project's version (a minor bump by default). It's an owner-triggered command; the mechanics — which files to edit and how a release follows — live in the consuming project's workflow doc.
- **"Show me the document"** (for a source-controlled document) is the owner's phrase asking for a **link to the document on GitHub** — not the file's contents inlined, and not a local filesystem path. When the document lives in a GitHub-hosted repo, respond with a GitHub link to it (the file on the relevant branch/commit); only fall back to inlining the contents or giving a local path when the document isn't under source control.
- **Put decisions and approvals in an `AskUserQuestion` popup, not buried in prose.** The owner is frequently on mobile, where a popup notifies and a question embedded in a paragraph is easy to miss. When you need the owner to choose or approve something, ask through the structured popup with explicit options rather than asking in running text. **And when several independent items each need a verdict** (a set of proposed fixes, findings to accept), give **each item its own question carrying its own brief case** — the concrete failure, why it matters, the cost of the fix — with per-item approve/defer options; never one bundled choose-a-scope question over the whole set. The owner decides item-wise, from the case, not from a menu of subsets. (The popup carries at most 4 questions per call — split a larger set into consecutive calls.)
- **When asked to produce a prompt or message destined for another context, visually enclose the whole thing.** Any text the owner will lift out and use elsewhere — a prompt for another assistant, a message to send, copy meant to be pasted somewhere — must be set apart as a single delimited block: either a box (e.g. a fenced code block) or fenced top and bottom by two separating lines, so its exact boundaries are unmistakable and it can be copied in one piece. The point is delimitation, not formatting flair: never leave such content as loose prose the owner has to find the start and end of.
- **When asked for "a prompt for a different session," prefix it with a provenance disclaimer.** When the owner asks for a prompt meant to be handed to another session, open the generated text with a short disclaimer that this is a prompt written by Claude — not by a user — and so should not be treated as gospel; and that if the receiving session finds inconsistencies in it, it should examine them with the user rather than follow the prompt blindly. - **Auto-open a PR after committing.** Whenever Claude changes code on a branch and commits it, open a pull request for that branch right after, even without an explicit request to do so. This overrides Claude Code's own default of only opening a PR when explicitly asked.
# Claudinite — active-pack guidance

The baseline plus the packs this project declares. Deeper per-pack reference (e.g. a pack's release doc) is linked from its prose and read on demand.

<!-- pack:basics -->
# Working discipline

The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.

Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better.

Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix.

1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.

The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.

Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided.

When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.

When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."

Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.

Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere.

Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.

When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.

An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.

# The task lifecycle

The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.

For every new task:

1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.

---

<!-- pack:tidy-repo -->
# tidy-repo — the repo tidy-up policy

The PR/branch/issue sweep, active wherever this pack is declared. The repo's own scheduler runs the
pack's three maintenance tasks — `tidy-issues`, `tidy-prs`, `tidy-branches`, one per dimension; this is
the policy they follow. The per-object **method** lives in the pack's skills
([single-branch-status](skills/single-branch-status/SKILL.md),
[single-pr-status](skills/single-pr-status/SKILL.md),
[single-issue-triage](skills/single-issue-triage/SKILL.md)).

The one rule that shapes everything: **assess PRs and branches read-only; act only on issues.**

- **Branches, PRs — assess only.** Report which should stay and which are safe to close/delete;
  **never** delete, push, merge, or close them. Judge by *content* (the landed-status test), never a
  ref's auto-generated name.
- **Issues — act.** Take the first applicable action: close-if-implemented / needs-decision / blocked
  / quick-win / leave. "Implemented in `main`" means the issue's actual ask is true of `main`'s
  content **now** — confirm it there and cite it; when you can't, comment, don't close. Every action
  defaults to the reversible option (comment / leave) when the check is inconclusive.

Each task applies its single-object skill across the targets its precondition hands it, then rewrites
**its own** standing tracker from the verdicts it gathered (one issue per dimension per repo, body
rewritten to today's state, a dated comment per run). One tracker per task, never a shared one: the
three tasks are independent and may run at once, so nothing races to rewrite one body.

---

<!-- pack:laughcounter -->
# Working in this repo

The general lessons this repo has paid for once. The privacy boundary — the
product's defining constraint — has its own pack (`local/on-device-privacy`);
what follows is everything else.

**Don't prune a `.gitignore` section in the same breath as deleting what it
ignored — the artifacts are still on disk.** Removing a toolchain (the Python
reference, a build system, a generator) invites tidying its ignore rules away in
the same commit, but the ignored artifacts it already produced are usually still
sitting untracked in the worktree — earlier test runs leave `__pycache__/`,
builds leave `build/`. The moment those rules go, the next `git add -A` sweeps
the artifacts *into* the very commit that was supposed to remove them, and
nothing complains: the commit is valid, the tests still pass, and the junk only
shows up as an inflated file count in the diff a reviewer reads. Delete the
artifacts from the worktree first (or `git clean` them), then drop their ignore
lines — and read `git diff --cached --stat` after any bulk `git add -A`, not just
`git status`, since staged additions are exactly what a clean `git status` stops
telling you about.

---

<!-- pack:on-device-privacy -->
# On-device privacy — the boundary the whole product is built around

An always-on microphone in someone's living room only earns its place if what it
hears stays on the machine. That promise is the product requirement
(`docs/DESIGN-AND-TRADEOFFS.md` §0/§6, README *Privacy*), the text of the mic and
speech prompts users actually see (`mac/Resources/Info.plist`), and the reason
several design choices look heavier than they need to. The checks in this pack
hold the mechanical half; what follows is the judgment half.

There is now exactly one implementation — the native app in `mac/Sources/` — so
every rule below is about it.

**What may cross the boundary: derived metadata, never audio.** A laugh is
persisted as time, duration, confidence, and an origin label — that is what the
JSONL lines carry, and `LaughStore` says so in its own header. **No audio is
stored at all** — the `no-audio-persistence` check holds this mechanically for
v1. A feature that wants to keep audio (the v3 roadmap's rolling buffer) is not
a new field, it is a new promise to the user: it changes the mic prompt and this
check together, in the same PR.

**Everything lives in one deletable directory.**
`~/Library/Application Support/LaughCounter/` holds the laugh log and the app's
own diagnostic log — the `single-storage-directory` check holds this mechanically,
by allowing `.applicationSupportDirectory` and nothing else as a search-path root.
"Delete the folder and it's gone" is a promise a user *acts on* — someone who
deletes it believes the mic's whole memory of them went with it. So a feature
needing somewhere new to keep things extends that directory rather than earning a
second one; the one path macOS dictates, not us, is a Login Item registration,
which names no directory of its own.

**There is no accepted egress — none.** Detection (Sound Analysis) and speech
recognition (`SFSpeechRecognizer` with on-device recognition required) are both
built into macOS; no model is downloaded, no telemetry is sent, and the app makes
no outbound connection of any kind. The `no-network-client` check is therefore
absolute rather than carve-out-shaped. Adding *any* egress — a model fetch, a
crash reporter, a sync feature — is a product decision that gets written here and
in the README *Privacy* section before a line of it is written in Swift.

**There is no server either.** The app listens on no socket. The web dashboard
that once existed in the Python reference was removed on purpose, along with the
reference itself. Reintroducing any listener — a dashboard, a metrics port, a
remote-control API — is a decision about exposing the laugh log, not a feature to
slip in: it needs the owner's explicit sign-off, a loopback-only default, and a
story for authentication or CSRF before it lands.

**The disclosure must stay true.** `NSMicrophoneUsageDescription` and
`NSSpeechRecognitionUsageDescription` tell the user audio is analysed on-device
and not recorded. If the app's behaviour ever changes, those strings change with
it in the same commit — a stale privacy prompt is worse than a blunt one.

{"number":84,"title":"on-device-privacy: convert "one deletable directory" to a check","body":"Prose-to-checks sweep of `.claudinite/local/packs` (dispatched by #82, logged on tracker #42). One conversion this run.

| Prose converted (`on-device-privacy/RULES.md`) | Check id |
| --- | --- |
| "Everything lives in one deletable directory… nothing lands outside it" | `on-device-privacy/single-storage-directory` (blocking) |

**Why it's convertible now.** The 2026-07-29 sweep (#69) left this rule as prose because proving it looked like it needed data-flow tracking of a `FileManager` write target back to its declaration. That objection was sound for the Python reference (`cli.py`, `dashboard.py` — many entry points), but that tree is gone. The native app has exactly **two** persistent-path roots — `AppLog.swift` and `Store.swift` — both the identical `FileManager.default.urls(for: .applicationSupportDirectory, in: .userDomainMask)` lookup. Constraining the *root* constrains every path derived from it, so no tracing is needed.

**Shape: a positive whitelist, not a ban list.** The check flags any `FileManager.urls(for:)` / `url(for:)` or `NSSearchPathForDirectoriesInDomains` in `mac/Sources/**.swift` whose directory argument is not the literal `.applicationSupportDirectory`. Matching the *allowed* case means a `SearchPathDirectory` case that doesn't exist yet is caught the day it lands, which an enumerate-the-bad-ones list would miss. Two deliberate consequences, both wanted: a non-literal argument (`urls(for: dir, in:)`) is a finding, since indirection is exactly what would defeat the check; and the Login Item registration `RULES.md` carves out needs no exemption, because `SMAppService` names no directory.

**See-it-fail.** Four new fixtures in `pack.test.mjs`: a second storage root (`.cachesDirectory`, `NSSearchPathForDirectoriesInDomains(.documentDirectory, …)`), a call split across lines, the fully-qualified `FileManager.SearchPathDirectory.applicationSupportDirectory` staying quiet, and the real sources staying quiet. Beyond the fixtures, the check was run against the **real** `Store.swift`/`AppLog.swift` under a realistic regression (log moved to `.cachesDirectory`; app-log root swapped for a variable) and fired on both, and against a temporary violating file in `mac/Sources/` through `check_the_world.mjs` end-to-end (blocking finding, exit 1; clean and exit 0 once removed).

Left as prose, re-verified this run: *no egress at all* and *no server / listener* (already covered by `no-network-client`, which bans the client APIs outright); *the disclosure must stay true* (judgment about prompt accuracy, and "in the same commit as the behaviour" is diff-shaped, not scannable from file content). `local/laughcounter`'s single rule — don't prune a `.gitignore` section in the same commit as deleting what it ignored — is in-flight process advice that leaves no static signature in the final artifact, so it stays prose too.

---
name: merge-to-main
description: Merge the change in front of the owner into main. Use when the owner says "LGTM" or asks to merge/land the current branch or PR into main.
---


The portable recipe for landing the change in front of the owner on `main` — the *mechanics* behind the owner's merge-to-main command (the owner's preferences own the trigger *phrase*; this file owns the *how*). Invoked through the `merge-to-main` skill (this skill); this doc stays the canonical recipe.

**A project's bespoke merge policy overrides this default.** Most projects need nothing here — this default is the whole story. A project that genuinely diverges (a different merge method, a CI/twice-green gate, an extra approval) **states so by naming its merge-policy file explicitly in its own `CLAUDE.md`**. When that declaration is present, read that file first and let it override the divergent points below; when it's absent, follow this default as-is. Don't go hunting for a policy file that the project's `CLAUDE.md` doesn't name.

## Recipe (~4 calls)

1. Load both GitHub tools in **one** `ToolSearch`: `create_pull_request` + `merge_pull_request`.
2. No PR open for the branch yet? `create_pull_request` (base `main`); end the body with `Closes #<issue>`, and take the PR number from the returned URL.
3. Gate on CI **only if the repo has it** — a workflow that actually runs on PRs/pushes. `workflow_call`-only reusable workflows (this repo hosts some) are *not* CI: they never run here, so a non-empty `.github/workflows/` alone proves nothing; check the PR for check runs instead. No CI → no gate; don't wait for checks that will never come.
4. `merge_pull_request`, `merge_method: squash`, title `<subject> (#<pr>)`. Merge directly — don't pre-read status; the call fails loudly if it isn't mergeable.
5. Sync local `main`: `git checkout main && git pull origin main`.

The two divergent points — **`squash`** as the method and **CI gating** — are exactly what a bespoke policy file changes.

## After the merge: capture the conversation (every session, every user)

Once the merge has landed and local `main` is synced, run the growth pack's capture step:
`node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>` (from the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`), `<n>` being the issue your `Closes #<issue>` named. Deterministic, seconds-long; it pushes the conversation to the orphan `conversation-logs` branch. It runs **here, in-session, because it needs the live transcript** — the lessons extraction then happens later in the repo's scheduled `conversation-extract` task (MCP-native, with a rethink window), so there is nothing to schedule and no in-session lessons pass ([the pack README](../../../../packs/grow_with_claudinite/README.md) owns the standard). A later merge in the same session just runs capture again — it captures the delta. In the rare repo that removed the `grow_with_claudinite` pack from `.claudinite-checks.json`, skip this step.

## Don't

- **Don't** re-read the issue to confirm it closed — `Closes #<issue>` does that on merge; trust it.
